meta.title: Tariqa Maryamiyya — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the Maryamiyya and the Traditionalist School (1886–present)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of the Tariqa Maryamiyya — the Sufi order founded by Frithjof Schuon — and the wider Traditionalist School (Guénon–Schuon perennialism), with special attention to its documented connections: to Catholic traditionalism and to Brazil.
meta.dataQualityNote: This is a work-in-progress dataset about a semi-private initiatic order and, in part, living people. It is compiled only from published scholarship (Mark Sedgwick's work is the academic backbone) and participants' own public writings; sympathetic, critical and apostate sources are labeled as such; contested characterizations are attributed, never asserted in the site's own voice; dates the sources dispute are flagged with a ? mark; and no private individuals are named. Corrections against published sources are welcome.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A Sufi order ([[tariqa]]) of Western origin founded by Frithjof Schuon, and the organizational heart of the [[traditionalist-school|Traditionalist School]] — the perennialist current of René Guénon, Schuon and Ananda Coomaraswamy.

facts.label: Lineage
facts.value: A branch of the Alawiyya of Shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi (Mostaganem, Algeria), where Schuon was initiated in the early 1930s; Schuon assumed the function of independent shaykh in Basel in late 1936 — an investiture his followers describe as divinely confirmed and Sedgwick treats as self-authorization. Sedgwick (14 July 2010) places the order twice over. Organizationally it is, in his words, “an independent branch of the Alawiyya, which is itself an independent branch of the Darqawiyya, which is itself an independent branch of the Shadhiliyya” — “independent” meaning that it operates independently of the tariqa it derives from and that its practice, prayers and teachings differ in certain respects, which he notes is true of most tariqas in existence today. Personally, Schuon is “a link in a chain ([[silsila]])” passing through Ahmad al-Alawi, Muhammad al-Arabi al-Darqawi and Abu’l-Hasan al-Shadhili, and then through both Ali ibn Abi Talib and Abu Bakr to the Prophet Muhammad.

facts.label: The name
facts.value: 'Maryamiyya' — after the Virgin Mary (Maryam), whom Schuon regarded as the order's spiritual protectress following visions he reported in 1965; the name was formally added in 1969 (full style: Tariqa Shadhiliyya-Darqawiyya-Alawiyya-Maryamiyya).

facts.label: Headquarters
facts.value: Lausanne, Switzerland (1941–1980), then Bloomington, Indiana (1980–1998); since Schuon's retirement and death, autonomous zawiyas under individual khalifas — commonly described as Washington (Nasr) and London (Lings) branches, though Wikipedia's account stresses that no successor was named.

facts.label: In Brazil
facts.value: A Brazilian branch founded in 1986/87 (sources differ) — described as the first tariqa brought to Brazil by Brazilians — with Olavo de Carvalho as Schuon's muqaddam until his break with Schuon at the end of the 1980s; centers reported at São José dos Campos (SP) with branch affiliations still to be verified.

facts.label: Why it is in this project family
facts.value: The documented crossovers: Rama Coomaraswamy — per Sedgwick never a formal Maryamiyya member, but a personal follower of Schuon who led a Catholic group practicing dhikr-like prayer with Christian concepts; also an SSPX seminary professor and sedevacantist priest — bridges to the fsspx project; Olavo de Carvalho (Maryami muqaddam turned philosopher of the Brazilian right) bridges to the fsp project's critical literature.

events.title: Guénon's Sufi affiliation
events.text: René Guénon adopts Islam in the Shadhili lineage transmitted through Ivan Aguéli (Abd al-Hadi); sources date the affiliation 1912 and the initiation itself variously c. 1910–1912.

events.title: 'Le Théosophisme'
events.text: Guénon publishes his critical history of the Theosophical Society — the Traditionalist critique of modern 'counter-tradition' begins in print.

events.title: 'Orient et Occident'
events.text: Guénon's book marks his break with the French Catholic intellectuals among whom he had first written.

events.title: 'La Crise du monde moderne'
events.text: Guénon publishes the school's most famous statement of civilizational critique.

events.title: Guénon moves to Cairo
events.text: He lives there as Abd al-Wahid Yahya until his death, marrying Fatima Ibrahim (1934) and taking Egyptian citizenship (1949).

events.title: Schuon initiated in the Alawiyya
events.text: Frithjof Schuon enters Islam and is initiated at the [[zawiya]] of Shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi, receiving the name Isa Nur ad-Din; Wikipedia's own articles date the stay 1932 or 1933–34 — the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved.

events.title: Schuon made muqaddam
events.text: Per Wikipedia's account, Shaykh Adda ben Tounes, al-Alawi's successor, authorizes Schuon to initiate aspirants into the Alawi order in Europe; the 1935 dating rests on that single tertiary source and is not corroborated here. Whether and how Schuon was authorized as a [[muqaddam]] is itself disputed, and Sedgwick (14 July 2010) declines to make it decisive: setting out where the Maryamiyya sits in Sufi classification, he writes that “the question of whether or not (or how) Schuon was authorized as a muqaddam by al-Alawi has no bearing or impact on” Schuon's place in the [[silsila]]. The disagreement is recorded, not resolved.

events.title: Independent shaykh
events.text: Schuon assumes the function of shaykh of an independent branch. Followers' accounts describe a divine investiture confirmed by disciples' dreams; Sedgwick treats it as self-authorization — both framings are attributed.

events.title: The order settles in Lausanne
events.text: Schuon directs the order from Lausanne for four decades (1941–1980).

events.title: The Plains Indian dimension begins
events.text: After reading 'Black Elk Speaks', Schuon initiates contact with Lakota tradition-holders; he and his wife are later adopted into the Sioux family of Chief James Red Cloud (1959) and by Thomas Yellowtail into the Crow (1984).

events.title: 'The Transcendent Unity of Religions'
events.text: Schuon publishes his best-known statement of perennialism (English translation 1953).

events.title: The Vâlsan split
events.text: Per Sedgwick: disciples object to Schuon's relaxation of Islamic practice; Guénon encourages Michel Vâlsan to separate the Paris branch, and Vâlsan establishes an independent, sharia-observant Alawiyya line with Guénon's approval.

events.title: The Marian visions
events.text: Schuon reports visions of the Virgin Mary ('Marian graces') and thereafter regards Mary as the order's spiritual protectress — the origin of the order's distinctive Marian devotion. Sedgwick (14 July 2010) ties the order's foundation as a distinct tariqa to “the authorization said to have been given to Schuon in a vision by the Virgin Mary”, paralleling it with the authorization “said to have been given to al-Alawi in a vision by Ali ibn Abi Talib” and adding that “while such forms of authorization are not universal, they are very common.” His conclusion is deliberately conditional: “the Maryamiyya is probably ‘valid’ to the extent that Schuon’s vision of the Virgin Mary in 1965 was ‘valid.’” Answering a commenter the same day, he stressed that he had expressed no view on whether the vision was valid.

events.title: Bloomington chapter founded
events.text: Indiana University professor Victor Danner founds the Bloomington chapter, which becomes the order's most important American center.

events.title: 'Maryamiyya' enters the name
events.text: The order formally becomes the Tariqa Shadhiliyya-Darqawiyya-Alawiyya-Maryamiyya.

events.title: Huston Smith joins
events.text: The scholar of world religions joins the order after meeting Schuon, attending his first [[dhikr]] in Tehran — with Nasr, one of the two most famous academic followers per Sedgwick.

events.title: Schuon moves to Bloomington
events.text: Schuon and his wife emigrate from Lausanne to Bloomington, where a large community of disciples already lived; the publishing house World Wisdom is founded there the same year.

events.title: Nasr's Washington platform
events.text: Seyyed Hossein Nasr becomes University Professor of Islamic Studies at George Washington University and founds the Foundation for Traditional Studies, publisher of the journal Sophia.

events.title: The Brazilian branch founded
events.text: Olavo de Carvalho leads a group of Brazilians to Bloomington, is initiated (taking the name Sidi Muhammad Ibrahim, per the critical documentary blog, corroborated in outline by Sedgwick), and is appointed [[muqaddam]] in Brazil under Martin Lings's guidance — described as the first tariqa brought to Brazil by Brazilians. Sources split between 1986 (Sedgwick) and 1987 (Brazilian tertiary sources) for the founding. Sedgwick's later obituary notice (28 Jan 2022) calls him "briefly a Maryami and the [[khalifa]] of Frithjof Schuon in Brazil", where this dataset and the Brazilian sources say [[muqaddam]]; the two titles are distinct and the divergence is recorded, not resolved. Carvalho's own dated account, in the Curso Online de Filosofia, adds a fourth voice to this record without settling it. In aula 094 (12 February 2011) he said that as soon as he entered Schuon's tariqa he was immediately appointed its [[muqaddam]] — which he glossed as the organization's representative for Brazil — that he had not asked for the post and found the speed of the appointment odd, and that the order then passed its instructions to a different man, creating a conflict of authority he described as dishonest. In aula 033 (21 November 2009) he said that at the time of the essays collected in Universalidade e Abstração (1983) he was an aspirant who later became a member, that he wrote in the manner of the Études Traditionnelles circle in order to please the shaykh, and that he was accepted at the first attempt while others had been applying yearly for twelve years. His self-description as [[muqaddam]] agrees with this dataset and the Brazilian sources and not with Sedgwick's obituary notice, which says [[khalifa]]; a participant's self-disclosure does not adjudicate a scholarly source, and the divergence stays recorded rather than resolved. None of this is quoted: the corpus text is a community transcription unchecked against the audio.

events.title: Olavo breaks with Schuon
events.text: Olavo de Carvalho leaves the order after a rupture with Schuon; the sources disagree on the date — 1987 (Bunker da Cultura), 'the late 1980s' (Sedgwick), or an expelled-1987–91 window (the Jardim series) — and on the reasons, with his own published framing (the multiconfessional rule, in 'Influências discretas') differing from the hostile accounts; every version is attributed. He reinvents himself, in Sedgwick's phrase, as a Catholic-identifying 'post-Traditionalist'. Carvalho's own tellings in the Curso Online de Filosofia are a fourth attributed account, and they diverge from each other, which is itself the finding. In aula 094 (12 February 2011) he framed the ending as his own act — when he broke with these people, he said, they activated the order's customary judicial harassment, inventing a case accusing him of a crime he had not committed which cost him six years and nearly ruined him before he won it; he added that the accusation he suffered came at forty (he was born in 1947), and that all of it was more than twenty years earlier. In aula 218 (31 August 2013), reading out a critic's summary that had him expelled from the Maryamiyya, he said that this checked out perfectly, that he had already explained the circumstances, and that he holds the whole correspondence; in the same lecture he said that one cannot leave a tariqa of one's own accord — either the man puts you out or you never leave. In aula 241 (1 March 2014) he repeated the six-year lawsuit and said the order's usual practice was judicial harassment, which it could not press further in Brazil because it had only eight disciples there. Break-by-his-own-act and expulsion are not the same claim, and he made both; the year remains unfixed and the dateVerified flag stays down. Nothing here is quoted — the corpus text has not been checked against the audio.

events.title: The Bloomington affair — indictment and dismissal
events.text: A grand jury indicts Schuon, 84, on allegations by a former member concerning ritual gatherings; the judge criticizes the indictment as vague (Bloomington press coverage of 29 October 1991), and on 20 November the county prosecutor dismisses all charges, stating there was insufficient evidence — 'not one shred of evidence' beyond the complainant's allegations, per the wording quoted by Wikipedia — adding that a miscarriage had occurred insofar as Schuon had been labeled. Schuon was never tried and the case was never revived. In announcing the dismissal, prosecutor Robert Miller said the deputy prosecutor who had headed the grand jury investigation, David Hunter, 'has submitted his resignation' and had resigned his position 'last week', and declined to say whether he had requested it; Hunter for his part blamed Miller (contemporaneous Bloomington coverage as reproduced by accuratenews.net, a pro-Schuon archive, labeled as such). Critical accounts instead say Hunter was fired; both versions are attributed. One hostile ex-member's view of the allegation is on the record twice and is not what might be expected: in the Curso Online de Filosofia, aula 094 (12 February 2011) and again in aula 241 (1 March 2014), Carvalho — who in the same breath declares his own resentment against Schuon and describes a lawsuit the order's disciples brought against him — said he does not believe the pedophilia accusation, and in aula 241 attributed it to a man who had had an affair with one of Schuon's wives, was expelled, and wrote violently against him. He is an interested witness whose account of the complainant is unverified here and is recorded as his claim, not as a finding; it is noted because it comes from the order's critic, not its defenders.

events.title: Schuon retires
events.text: Aged 85, Schuon resigns the direction of the order — per Wikipedia, without naming a successor, establishing instead independent zawiyas led by individual [[khalifa|khalifas]].

events.title: Death of Frithjof Schuon
events.text: The order continues in autonomous branches, commonly identified with Seyyed Hossein Nasr (Washington) and Martin Lings (London) — a framing that coexists with the no-named-successor account. A fourth account exists and disagrees with the no-named-successor framing: in the Curso Online de Filosofia, aula 041 (16 January 2010), Carvalho said that when Schuon died Martin Lings became shaykh of the tariqa shortly afterwards, and described the office in strong terms — a shaykh has no friends, only disciples. In aula 209 (29 June 2013) he gave a different emphasis, saying Schuon's tariqa dissolved after his death amid scandals and quarrels and that several tariqas emerged from it, the principal one being, in his account, of strict Islamic observance despite the universalist language of its discourse. Both are his attributed characterizations; neither is corroborated here, and the Wikipedia-sourced account above is not displaced by them.

events.title: Death of Rama Coomaraswamy
events.text: The perennialist author, cardiac surgeon, sometime SSPX seminary professor and sedevacantist priest dies at 76 — the single most documented bridge between this order's world and Catholic traditionalism.

events.title: Olavo honored with Bannon and Bolsonaro
events.text: Olavo de Carvalho is honored at a dinner with Steve Bannon and President Jair Bolsonaro — the moment the Brazilian ex-Maryami's political influence becomes an international story; Sedgwick calls him Brazil's most prominent post-Traditionalist.

events.title: Borella publishes his critique of Guénon and Schuon
events.text: Jean Borella publishes 'Ésotérisme guénonien et mystère chrétien' (L'Âge d'Homme, coll. Delphica; English translation 'Guénonian Esoterism and Christian Mystery', Sophia Perennis, 2004) — his public critique of Guénon's thesis on the Christian sacraments and of Schuon's supra-confessional esoterism. The Schuonian editorial by Renaud Fabbri (critical of Borella, labeled) reads him as having 'progressively distanced himself' from the school. Sources describe this departure as a gradual distancing rather than a dated break; this publication is its clearest datable public marker.

events.title: Public polemic over 'Christian Hermeticism' and perennialist influence
events.text: A multi-round public dispute among traditionalist-Catholic writers over 'Christian Hermeticism' and perennialist influence in traditionalist-Catholic publishing, running from June 2025 into January 2026. Michael Warren Davis (WM Review, 3 June 2025) and Thomas V. Mirus (CatholicCulture, 5 June 2025 — invoking the Rama Coomaraswamy precedent) criticized Sebastian Morello's book on Christian Hermeticism; Morello replied (OnePeterFive, 11 June 2025); Chris Jackson (Big Modernism, 13 June 2025) pressed the critique against Morello's defenders; and John Lamont and Morello exchanged further replies at Rorate Caeli (December 2025–January 2026). Each characterization is its named author's and this site takes no side on any accusation; the exchange is chronicled here only for its dated course, as the perennialist crossover seen from the Catholic-traditionalist side — the per-person accusations belong, minimally and BLP-grade, to the fsspx project's orbit.

figures.name: René Guénon (Abd al-Wahid Yahya)
figures.role: Founder of the Traditionalist School; French metaphysician, Cairo-based Sufi from 1930; backed Vâlsan's 1950 separation from Schuon's branch.

figures.name: Frithjof Schuon (Isa Nur ad-Din Ahmad)
figures.role: Founder and shaykh of the branch that became the Maryamiyya (1936–1992); leading perennialist author ('The Transcendent Unity of Religions').

figures.name: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy
figures.role: Art historian (Boston Museum of Fine Arts); with Guénon and Schuon one of the school's three founding authors. Exact biographical dates to verify.

figures.name: Rama P. Coomaraswamy
figures.role: Son of Ananda; cardiac surgeon, later psychiatrist; professor of ecclesiastical history at the SSPX's St. Thomas Aquinas seminary at Ridgefield, Connecticut 'for five years' — that is, until about 1983 — per the 2007 memorial by William Stoddart and Mateus Soares de Azevedo, which says nothing further about his part in the Society's internal disputes. The stronger claim in circulation, that he drew the future SSPV founders to [[sedevacantism]], rests on a mirror of a since-deleted Wikipedia article alone and is recorded here as unverified (to verify) — Fr. Anthony Cekada's own account of the 1983 split does not mention him; the fsspx project carries that dispute. Sedevacantist priest ordained in 1999 by Bishop José Ramón López-Gastón of the Thục line (per his own published account); contributor to the Foundation for Traditional Studies' journal Sophia. Per Sedgwick (Against the Modern World, p. 161) he was never a formal Maryamiyya member but a personal follower of Schuon who led a Catholic group practicing dhikr-like repetitive prayer with Christian concepts — see the fsspx project's dossier.

figures.name: Titus Burckhardt (Ibrahim Izz ad-Din)
figures.role: Swiss author on sacred art and civilization; Schuon's closest lifelong collaborator.

figures.name: Martin Lings (Abu Bakr Siraj ad-Din)
figures.role: British Arabist and Shakespeare scholar, author of the celebrated 'Muhammad' (1983); head of the order's London line; advised the founding of the Brazilian branch. Olavo de Carvalho, who was in the order in the 1980s, described him from personal acquaintance in the Curso Online de Filosofia: in aula 036 (12 December 2009) he named Lings among the few teachers he had and said he had known him and counted him a friend; in aula 041 (16 January 2010) he said he had corresponded with Lings for a long time and later met him in Peru, called him a great man and his Muhammad a masterpiece, and at the same time said Lings was a Muslim conducting a strategic action on behalf of Islam and that the Prince of Wales became his disciple after writing a preface to Lings's book on Shakespeare — an attributed political reading, not a finding, and separable from the biographical detail. In the same lectures he twice calls Lings a former director of the British Museum; Lings was Keeper of Oriental Manuscripts and Printed Books there, not its director, and the error is noted as a caution on the reliability of these lectures about other people's lives. Carvalho also said (aula 041) that Lings became shaykh of the tariqa shortly after Schuon's death — see the 1998 entry, where that claim sits beside the no-named-successor account rather than replacing it. Nothing is quoted: the corpus text is a community transcription unchecked against the audio.

figures.name: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
figures.role: University Professor of Islamic Studies at George Washington University (from 1984); founder of the Foundation for Traditional Studies; head of the order's Washington line; the school's most prominent academic voice. Carvalho met him and assessed him twice, differently, in the Curso Online de Filosofia: in aula 228 (16 November 2013) he described Nasr's Iranian upbringing and MIT training with admiration and said that on meeting him he found not only great learning but an intrinsic nobility of presence he had rarely seen; in aula 241 (1 March 2014) he called Nasr's history-of-science work wholly disinterested and his expositions of Sufism faithful, while judging his later books ideological propaganda for Schuon. In the same 2014 lecture he reported — as hearsay, on which he did not vouch — that after Schuon's tariqa ended Nasr was said to head a new one while another sector followed a different man. All of this is his attributed opinion; it does not displace the published scholarship above, and nothing is quoted from an audio-unverified transcription.

figures.name: Michel Vâlsan (Mustafa Abd al-Aziz)
figures.role: Romanian diplomat and esoterist; led the Paris Alawiyya and separated it from Schuon's branch in 1950 with Guénon's approval, founding the sharia-observant 'Guénonian-orthodox' line; editor of Études Traditionnelles. Exact biographical dates to verify. Carvalho's account of the same split, in the Curso Online de Filosofia, aula 209 (29 June 2013), is consistent with this in outline and adds a name: he said the tariqas that had formed divided in two, between 'guénonistas' and the 'perenialistas' who followed Schuon, that the Guénonian half closed its orders to non-Muslims and required full observance of the sharia, and that roughly half of them were led above all by Vâlsan — a Romanian — and afterwards by Charles-André Gilis. Gilis is not otherwise documented in this dataset; the succession is recorded as Carvalho's attributed claim. An undated lecture (aula 414, no date recoverable from the file) gives a much more colourful account of how Vâlsan came to Guénon; it is not cited here because it cannot be dated and has not been checked against audio.

figures.name: Victor Danner
figures.role: Indiana University professor who founded the Bloomington chapter (1967), seeding the community that became the order's headquarters. Biographical dates to verify.

figures.name: Whitall Perry
figures.role: American compiler of 'A Treasury of Traditional Wisdom'; member of Schuon's circle in Lausanne and Bloomington.

figures.name: Huston Smith
figures.role: Scholar of world religions ('The World's Religions'); joined the order in 1974 — with Nasr, its most famous academic follower per Sedgwick.

figures.name: Marco Pallis
figures.role: British-Greek mountaineer and author on Tibetan Buddhism; Traditionalist author. Biographical dates to verify.

figures.name: Thomas Yellowtail
figures.role: Crow Sun Dance chief and medicine man — the English Wikipedia article describes him as 'a medicine man for over thirty years'. Per the English Wikipedia article on Schuon he adopted Schuon into the Crow tribe in 1984, visited him every year and 'remained Schuon's intimate friend until his death in 1993' — the Plains Indian thread of the 1947 entry. No source located here documents any affiliation with the Maryamiyya or with any Sufi order: what is documented is the adoption and the friendship, not membership.

figures.name: Jean Borella
figures.role: French Catholic philosopher; professor of metaphysics and ancient/medieval philosophy at the University of Nancy (Nancy-II) from 1977 until his 1995 retirement. Long counted a Traditionalist and a personal follower of Schuon: per Sedgwick (Against the Modern World, p. 161) he 'led a subsidiary group of perhaps fifty Catholic Traditionalists', of whom Sedgwick writes 'None of these Christians were actually members of the Maryamiyya, but they followed Schuon personally as a Maryami would' — a follower, on this account, not an initiate. Long-time co-editor of the journal Connaissance des religions (per Sedgwick's blog, June 2022); Philitt (2017) calls him a 'disciple' of Schuon. He later distanced himself from the school — criticizing Guénon on the Christian sacraments and Schuon's 'supra-confessional esoterism'. No source found asserts a formal initiation. Carvalho read him the same way, from the other side: in the Curso Online de Filosofia, aula 043 (30 January 2010) he named Borella as one of the two or three people doing the work he thought necessary — absorbing the Guénon–Schuon legacy without prejudice and then asking what its relation to Christianity actually is — and singled out Borella's objection that the noun 'esoterism' has no ancient Greek ancestor at all; in aula 081 (30 October 2010) he said Borella began as a Guénonian of strict observance and that his later books are terribly anti-Guénonian, dismantling the thing from inside, and that he himself was learning to free himself from Guénon through Borella. Carvalho's characterizations are attributed and do not bear on the membership question, which no source in this dataset resolves in favour of initiation. The related Borella / Dom Basílio Méramo controversy that Carvalho described in aula 075 (18 September 2010) is recorded in the fsspx project, which owns the Catholic-traditionalist side; it is not duplicated here.

figures.name: James S. Cutsinger
figures.role: American scholar; Eastern Orthodox Christian; professor at the University of South Carolina (1980–2018) and editor/translator of several of Schuon's books. Per Sedgwick's blog (16 January 2023) he was 'a leading follower of Frithjof Schuon in a personal capacity, though never (as an Orthodox Christian) a formal member of the tariqa' — the same post associates him with Terry Moore and Hasan Awan's 2017 separation of a Washington–Baltimore branch. His documented office was secretary to the Foundation for Traditional Studies (a claim that he was 'Schuon's personal secretary' is unverified and not asserted here).

figures.name: Wolfgang Smith
figures.role: Austrian-American mathematician, physicist and Catholic perennialist author; published by Angelico Press, with his collected works carried by his Philos-Sophia Initiative. Documented intellectual engagement with Nasr — Nasr reviewed his 'The Quantum Enigma' in the journal Sophia (1997) — but no source documents membership of any Sufi order: his relation to the school is one of affinity, not initiation. Sacred Web (a perennialist journal — sympathetic, labeled) records that he wished to be remembered 'as a believing Christian' and attended the Tridentine Mass.

figures.name: Charles Upton
figures.role: American poet and metaphysical author; adjacent to the Maryamiyya but, by his own 2017 'Confession' (self-disclosure), never a member of it. He and his wife joined the Nimatullahi Sufi Order under Javad Nurbakhsh in 1988; his wife Jennifer was later initiated into the Maryamiyya through Schuon's muqaddam Seyyed Hossein Nasr, 'though I remained with the Nimatullahis'; from 2010 he became an initiate of a separate order in an 'Alawiyya-descended [[silsila]]. He writes critically on the Schuon-scandal era. Never to be described as an 'ex-Maryami' — adjacency is not initiation. A COF cross-reference of this dataset against the vaulted Curso Online de Filosofia corpus surfaces him in three lectures (aulas 342, 343 and 497), and one of them describes him in passing as a member of a Guénonian tariqa. That does not touch the record above and must not be read as Maryamiyya membership: all three files are in the corpus's unreviewed half, none carries a recoverable date, none has been checked against audio, and a third party's passing description is in any case not the kind of evidence this project accepts for membership — which requires self-disclosure or published scholarship. His own 2017 self-disclosure, that he was never a member of the Maryamiyya, stands. The lectures are noted here as a located lead, deliberately uncited, so that the mention is not later mistaken for new evidence.

figures.name: Olavo de Carvalho
figures.role: Brazilian essayist; joined the Maryamiyya in 1986, served as Schuon's muqaddam/khalifa in Brazil, broke with Schuon at the end of the 1980s, and became the Catholic-identifying philosopher of the Brazilian New Right — 'Brazil's most prominent post-Traditionalist' in Sedgwick's phrase; already documented as first-class critical literature in the sibling fsp project.

figures.name: Mateus Soares de Azevedo
figures.role: Brazilian perennialist author, journalist and translator into Portuguese of Schuon, Guénon, Lings, Stoddart and Rama Coomaraswamy; a World Wisdom author ('Men of a Single Book', 2010) and editor associated with the Schuonian/World Wisdom milieu. Felipe Souza's 2023 guest post calls him a 'prolific author' of 'Schuonian Traditionalism'. No membership of the Maryamiyya is self-disclosed or documented.

figures.name: Alberto Vasconcellos Queiroz
figures.role: Brazilian psychologist and public administrator in São José dos Campos; co-editor (with Mateus Soares de Azevedo) of William Stoddart's 'Remembering in a World of Forgetting' (World Wisdom, 2007) and a perennialist author in Portuguese. Any initiatic affiliation [U] — not self-disclosed and never inferred here.

organizations.name: Tariqa Alawiyya (parent order)
organizations.relation: The Shadhili-Darqawi order of Shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi (d. 1934), parent of both Schuon's branch and Vâlsan's Paris line.

organizations.name: Tariqa Maryamiyya
organizations.relation: Schuon's branch: independent from 1936, Marian in devotion from 1965, formally 'Maryamiyya' from 1969; headquartered in Lausanne 1941–1980 and Bloomington 1980–1998; decentralized after Schuon's retirement into autonomous zawiyas.

organizations.name: The Vâlsan / Paris line
organizations.relation: The independent, sharia-observant Alawiyya branch Michel Vâlsan established with Guénon's approval after objecting to Schuon's universalist adaptations — the 'Guénonian-orthodox' alternative within the same lineage; not Maryami.

organizations.name: Bloomington community
organizations.relation: Founded around Victor Danner's chapter; the order's world headquarters 1980–1998; the setting of the practices analyzed in Hugh Urban's study and of the 1991 affair (see the chronology's paired entry).

organizations.name: Washington branch (Nasr line)
organizations.relation: The line around Seyyed Hossein Nasr, George Washington University, and the Foundation for Traditional Studies (journal Sophia).

organizations.name: London branch (Lings line)
organizations.relation: The line around Martin Lings until his death in 2005.

organizations.name: Brazilian centers
organizations.relation: The branch founded under Olavo de Carvalho's muqaddam years. Per the abstract of Sedgwick's Aries article, two local groups developed in 1980s–90s Brazil — one restricting itself to Traditionalist doctrine, the other turning to T'ai chi and Brazilian indigenous religion rather than Sufism. Brazilian sources describe two centers — one at São José dos Campos (SP) — affiliated respectively to the London (Lings) and Washington (Nasr) lines; the full article (paywalled) is the key document to obtain (issue #1). Two size and structure claims come from Carvalho's own dated lectures and are recorded as his attributed account: in the Curso Online de Filosofia, aula 241 (1 March 2014) he said the order had only eight disciples in Brazil, and in aula 094 (12 February 2011) that although he had been appointed the organization's representative for Brazil, its instructions were being passed to another man — a parallel authority he described as dishonest. In the same 2011 lecture he said the Schuonian group in Brazil had helped organize a colloquium on Julius Evola through which Aleksandr Dugin first reached the country; that is Traditionalist politics rather than the order's initiatic line (see the disambiguation section) and is noted, not adopted.

organizations.name: Angelico Press / Sophia Perennis (publishers)
organizations.relation: The documented institutional bridge between Guénonian Traditionalism and traditional-Catholic publishing. Angelico Press was founded in the fall of 2011 by John Riess and James Wetmore (per Riess's own account, California Catholic Daily, 3 April 2013; both named as founders on the current about-us page). Wetmore is director of Sophia Perennis and translator/editor of volumes of the Collected Works of René Guénon. Mark Sedgwick (30 June 2022) describes Angelico as 'as much a (Guénonian) Traditionalist publisher that became popular among traditional Catholics as it was a traditional Catholic publisher that published (Guénonian) Traditionalists' — 'an overlap or even a mixing of two formerly distinct streams'. Sedgwick documents that in 2020 Angelico's site listed a joint Angelico Press / Sophia Perennis imprint (16 books) alongside a purely Sophia Perennis imprint (3 books), since removed from the site. The school-of-ideas side of Sophia Perennis is documented in the sibling perennialism project — linked here, not duplicated.
organizations.notes: Riess (2013) describes starting the press 'with two colleagues'; the current site names two founders — a possible third founder is unidentified (recorded, not resolved). sophiaperennis.com currently resolves to a parking page (observed 19 July 2026); live status unknown.

disambiguation.note: This subject sits at the crossing of three different things called 'traditionalism', a semi-private religious order, and living people. The entries below keep the wires uncrossed; every characterization is attributed.

items.title: Traditionalist School ≠ Catholic traditionalism
items.text: The Guénon–Schuon school (perennialism) is unrelated in origin to Catholic traditionalism (Lefebvre, Écône, [[sedevacantism]] — the fsspx project's subject). The documented bridges are individuals: Rama Coomaraswamy, Jean Borella, and Olavo de Carvalho. Guénon himself began among French Catholic intellectuals and broke with them ('Orient et Occident', 1924).

items.title: ≠ Evola's political 'Traditionalism'
items.text: Julius Evola adapted Guénon toward radical-right politics; Schuon's line was religious-initiatic, not political. The later Bannon/Dugin/alt-right 'Traditionalism' story connects to the Evolian reading — Sedgwick notes Olavo de Carvalho 'applied Guénon to political issues rather as Evola had, but unlike Evola combined Traditionalism with Roman Catholicism'. Attribute all such lineage claims.

items.title: Maryamiyya ≠ mainstream Sufism
items.text: Criticism of Schuon's universalist adaptations began inside the Guénonian world itself — the 1950 Vâlsan split over the relaxation of Islamic practice — and continued over the Marian devotion, the Plains Indian rites and the Bloomington gatherings. Defenders present these as legitimate esoteric adaptation; critics as syncretism. Both framings are attributed. On the narrower question of “validity”, Sedgwick (14 July 2010) argues the Maryamiyya can be placed like most tariqas — organizationally within the Alawiyya–Darqawiyya–Shadhiliyya descent, personally through Schuon's silsila — and concludes that “the Maryamiyya is probably ‘valid’ to the extent that Schuon’s vision of the Virgin Mary in 1965 was ‘valid.’” The formula is conditional by design and endorses neither side; it is quoted here as written.

items.title: Academic perennialism vs initiatic membership
items.text: Perennialism was taught openly in universities (Nasr, Smith) while tariqa membership remained private. This site keeps the published-scholarship layer separate from claims about membership, and carries no information about private living members — deceased figures and self-disclosed members only.

items.title: The 1991 Bloomington affair carries its resolution
items.text: Any mention of the 15 October 1991 indictment must carry the 20 November 1991 dismissal of all charges, the prosecutor's insufficient-evidence statements, and the fact that Schuon was never tried and the case never revived. The chronology's single paired entry is the pattern to follow.

items.title: Names and nicknames
items.text: 'Guru de Virgínia' is a Brazilian press nickname for Olavo de Carvalho (from his Virginia residence, 2005–2022), not a title about Schuon. The order's full style is Tariqa Shadhiliyya-Darqawiyya-Alawiyya-Maryamiyya; 'Maryamiyya' alone is standard in scholarship.

items.title: Follower ≠ member: the 'Christian Schuonians'
items.text: Sedgwick documents a category the record keeps flattening: Christians who followed Schuon personally without ever joining the tariqa — Rama Coomaraswamy's American Catholic group ('none of these Christians were actually members of the Maryamiyya'), probably Jean Borella's French circle, and the Orthodox scholar James Cutsinger, Schuon's editor, 'never (as an Orthodox Christian) a formal member'. Membership claims about individuals require self-disclosure or scholarship — adjacency is not initiation.

items.title: Brazil's Guénonian scene today (attributed to Felipe Souza, 2023)
items.text: A 2023 guest post by Felipe Souza on Mark Sedgwick's Traditionalists blog — authored by Souza, not Sedgwick — maps a Portuguese-language Guénonian milieu: the René Guénon Institute for Traditional Studies (IRGET), run by the late Luiz Pontual de Oliveira; translator-teachers Marcelo Cipolla and the História Islâmica portal (Mansur Peixoto); and Luiz Gonzaga de Carvalho, Olavo's son, said to attend the classes. These roles rest on Souza's single account and are recorded as attributed, not confirmed. Souza also situates Nova Resistência (Raphael Machado) as a Duginist movement that 'flirts with Guénonism' — that is Evola/Dugin-line political Traditionalism (the 'Fourth Political Theory'), kept apart from the Schuon school per this project's three-traditionalisms rule; it is not the Maryamiyya's initiatic line.

items.title: Olavo de Carvalho on his own tariqa years — a participant-witness whose tellings diverge
items.text: Between 2009 and 2014 Olavo de Carvalho talked about the Maryamiyya repeatedly in his Curso Online de Filosofia, and the vaulted corpus of that course (cronologia/archive, ADR-0005) lets those statements be cited by lecture number and lecture date rather than through a hostile channel's re-cut. Two rules govern how they are used here. First, he is a participant-witness on his own involvement and an attributed, interested voice on everyone else: in aula 218 (31 August 2013) he confirmed that he had belonged to Schuon's tariqa and that a critic's statement that he was expelled from it checked out perfectly, and in aula 094 (12 February 2011) that he was appointed [[muqaddam]] for Brazil as soon as he entered — self-disclosure, which this project accepts for his own membership. His characterizations of Nasr, Lings, Vâlsan, Borella and Upton are a different kind of claim and are carried attributed, beside the published scholarship, never in place of it. Second, his account does not adjudicate anything. On the date of the break, his own tellings do not even agree with each other: in 2011 he described leaving as his own act and dated the accusation that followed to his fortieth year, while in 2013 he accepted the word 'expelled'; that divergence is a fact about the source, and the 1986/87 founding and the end-of-the-1980s break stay flagged. On his title, his self-description as [[muqaddam]] agrees with the Brazilian sources and not with Sedgwick's obituary notice, which says [[khalifa]] — recorded as a divergence, not settled by a participant's word against a scholar's. One earlier datum belongs here too: in aula 019 (15 August 2009) he said he had come across Guénon's books in the 1970s and had read them all by about 1981 or 1982, which places his reading years before any of the dates above; the frequently repeated line in that same lecture claiming eyewitness standing among the tariqas is not his — it belongs to a student's letter he reads aloud, and is attributed here to that correspondent. Two further limits are worth stating plainly. Eleven of the lectures behind this section carry a date in the corpus manifest; several others that discuss the order at length carry none, because the corpus's unreviewed half has no headers to read a date from, and an identification without a date is a partial result that is not cited as a claim. And none of the wording is quoted anywhere in this dataset: the transcriptions are a community effort that has not been checked against the audio, so everything attributed to these lectures is paraphrase.

lineage.heading: Connections graph
lineage.note: The order's documented connections as a typed-edge graph. SOLID edges mark initiation or membership in the silsila; DASHED edges mark association or reference — a personal follower who was never a member, or a cross-link to a sibling project — and never imply initiation. Membership is asserted only where a source documents it; adjacency is never read as initiation, and every contested claim is attributed on its node.

Sedgwick adds that “the question of whether or not (or how) Schuon was authorized as a muqaddam by al-Alawi has no bearing or impact on this.” Organizationally he places the same descent as Maryamiyya < Alawiyya < Darqawiyya < Shadhiliyya, each an independent branch of the one before.

branchTimeline.heading: Branches over time
branchTimeline.note: The order's line and its divisions as a horizontal timeline — from the Alawiyya parentage through Schuon's independent branch, the Marian turn and the moves to Lausanne and Bloomington, to the autonomous post-1998 branches and the Brazilian branch and Olavo's break. Contested dates are flagged in the notes below and never resolved by preference.

trunk.label: Alawiyya → Schuon's Maryamiyya
trunk.note: A branch of the Alawiyya of Shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi: Schuon initiated c. 1932 (Wikipedia's articles date the stay 1932 or 1933–34 — recorded, not resolved), independent shaykh from 1936, Marian devotion from the reported 1965 visions, formally 'Maryamiyya' from 1969; directed from Lausanne 1941–1980 and Bloomington from 1980.

branches.label: Vâlsan / Paris line (not Maryami)
branches.note: Michel Vâlsan separated the Paris Alawiyya from Schuon's branch with Guénon's approval — the sharia-observant 'Guénonian-orthodox' line; not the Maryamiyya.

branches.label: Brazilian branch (Olavo, muqaddam → break)
branches.note: Olavo de Carvalho initiated at Bloomington and appointed muqaddam in Brazil — founding dated 1986 (Sedgwick) or 1987 (Brazilian sources); his break is dated 1987 (Bunker da Cultura), 'the late 1980s' (Sedgwick), or an expelled-1987–91 window (Jardim das Aflições) — a three-way disagreement recorded, not resolved.

branches.label: Brazilian centers (post-Olavo)
branches.note: After Olavo's departure, Brazilian centers (one at São José dos Campos) continued, per the abstract of Sedgwick's Aries article — one restricting itself to Traditionalist doctrine, the other turning to T'ai chi and indigenous religion; affiliations reported to the London (Lings) and Washington (Nasr) lines.

branches.label: Washington line (Nasr)
branches.note: One of the autonomous zawiyas after Schuon's retirement (1992) and death (1998), commonly associated with Seyyed Hossein Nasr — a framing that coexists with Wikipedia's no-named-successor account.

branches.label: London line (Lings)
branches.note: The autonomous line associated with Martin Lings until his death in 2005.

branches.label: Washington–Baltimore branch (2017 separation)
branches.note: Per Sedgwick (16 Jan 2023), a new and independent branch separated with Terry Moore and Hasan Awan; James Cutsinger is associated with it in Sedgwick's account (attributed).
